lessons.title: What Are Commodity Cycles and Why They Matter to Investors

children.text: Why Commodities Move in Cycles, Not Trends

Open a ten-year chart of Reliance Industries or HDFC Bank and you see, broadly, an upward slope interrupted by corrections. Open a ten-year chart of Brent crude, or MCX copper, or gold, and you see something else entirely: long stretches of dullness, punctuated by violent spikes and equally violent crashes, with no obvious growth trend underneath. That is the first thing to unlearn about investing in commodities. A company can grow its earnings every year for two decades. A barrel of oil cannot. It is worth roughly what it costs the marginal producer to pump it out of the ground, plus or minus a premium that depends entirely on how tight supply is relative to demand at that moment.

This course builds a framework for reading three of the most important commodity cycles for an Indian investor: crude oil, gold, and industrial metals such as copper, aluminium and steel. Each one moves for different reasons, and each one hits your portfolio, and the Indian economy, through a different channel. This lesson lays the foundation: what a commodity cycle actually is, why it looks so different from an equity cycle, and why ignoring it is expensive for anyone investing out of India.

body.text: Commodities do not compound. They cycle around the cost of producing them, and the amplitude of that cycle is the entire game.

children.text: The Commodity Cycle in Four Phases

Every commodity cycle, whether it plays out over eighteen months or fifteen years, moves through a similar sequence. The table below sketches the pattern using crude oil, the commodity we will study in depth in Chapter 2, as the running example.

body.caption: The Commodity Cycle, Phase by Phase (Crude Oil as Example)

cells: Oversupply / Trough
Prices fall below or near the cost of production. Producers cut capex, shut wells, delay projects.
Brent crude fell from around $100 a barrel in 2014 to near $30 by early 2016 as US shale supply overwhelmed demand.
Stabilisation
Supply growth slows as under-investment starts to bite. Demand keeps growing quietly in the background.
OPEC and Russia agreed repeated production cuts through 2017 to 2019 to drain the oversupply built up during the crash.
Demand Catches Supply
Inventories draw down, spare capacity shrinks, and prices start moving up sharply on relatively small demand or supply surprises.
Prices recovered through 2021 as global demand rebounded from the pandemic while producers stayed disciplined on new investment.
Boom / Peak
Prices spike well above the cost of production. Investors who were ignoring the commodity two years earlier now want exposure to it.
Brent spiked past $120 a barrel in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy supply.

body.text: Notice the pattern: the crash creates the conditions for the next boom, because under-investment eventually starves the market of supply. The boom then creates the conditions for the next crash, because high prices pull in new investment and force consumers to cut back. This is why commodity cycles are sometimes called self-correcting, and why extrapolating today's price into next year is usually the wrong instinct.

children.text: Why This Matters to an Indian Investor
A commodity cycle you are not watching does not stay out of your portfolio. It reaches you through three channels.

Inflation and interest rates: crude oil is India's single largest import bill. A sustained spike pushes up CPI, widens the current account deficit, weakens the rupee, and often forces the RBI's hand on rates, which affects every asset class, not just commodities.

Corporate earnings: entire NSE and BSE sectors are commodity price-takers. Oil marketing companies like Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL see their marketing margins squeezed when crude spikes. Metal companies like Tata Steel, Hindalco and JSW Steel see earnings swing directly with London Metal Exchange and domestic prices.

Direct portfolio exposure: whether you hold Sovereign Gold Bonds, a gold ETF, a commodity-linked mutual fund, or you trade futures on MCX through a broker like Zerodha, you are taking a cyclical bet whether you have framed it that way or not.

children.text: Why Commodities Don't Behave Like Stocks

markDefs.definition: The cost of the least efficient producer whose output the market still needs to meet demand. Over a full cycle, prices gravitate toward this number and spend most of their time near it.

children.text: A share of a well-run company can be worth more next year than this year because the business itself grows: more customers, more revenue, more profit reinvested at a decent return. A tonne of copper has no such internal engine. Whatever the world was willing to pay for it eventually gets pulled back toward one number: the
, and it only spikes meaningfully above that number when demand outruns available supply.

body.label: US Shale Breakeven Cost
body.context: The rough floor most analysts use for crude oil. Below this range, US shale producers start shutting in wells, which caps how far and how long a crash can run.

body.title: Quick Check: Reading the Cycle
body.question: Crude oil has just spiked to $110 a barrel after two years of underinvestment in new drilling. According to the four-phase framework, which phase is the market most likely in?
body.explanation: A sharp price spike well above the cost of production, following a period of underinvestment, is the signature of the Boom/Peak phase. This is usually also the point where capital rushes back into new supply, planting the seed for the next downturn.

body.title: Show me: how oil shocks show up in India's macro data

children.text: India imports well over four-fifths of the crude oil it consumes, so the oil price is one of the most closely watched inputs in Indian macro forecasting. A sustained $10 per barrel rise in the average annual price typically adds meaningfully to India's import bill, which widens the current account deficit and puts pressure on the rupee.

That pressure feeds into retail inflation within a few months, mainly through fuel and transport costs, and from there into freight and food prices. This is why the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee statements routinely flag crude oil as an explicit upside risk to the inflation outlook, and why a sudden oil spike can shift rate-cut expectations even when nothing else in the domestic economy has changed.

points: Commodities cycle around their cost of production. They do not compound the way equity earnings do.
Every commodity cycle broadly follows four phases: oversupply/trough, stabilisation, demand catching supply, and boom/peak, each one planting the seed for the next phase.

Commodity cycles reach Indian investors through three channels: inflation and rupee/RBI policy, commodity-linked sector earnings on the NSE and BSE, and direct exposure via SGBs, ETFs, and MCX contracts.
The next three chapters take crude oil, gold and industrial metals one at a time and build out how to read and act on each cycle.
